entries.321f29eea5c9ac99c4dd695dedd749cc0707c00f: <div sID="gen11208" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="45" osisID="Ps.45" sID="Ps.45"/> <div eID="gen11208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11209" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11210" type="x-p"/> This psalm is an illustrious prophecy of Messiah the Prince: it is all over gospel, and points at him only, as a bridegroom espousing the church to himself and as a king ruling in it and ruling for it. It is probable that our Saviour has reference to this psalm when he compares the kingdom of heaven, more than once, to a nuptial solemnity, the solemnity of a royal nuptial, <reference osisRef="Matt.22.2">Matt. xxii. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.25.1">xxv. 1</reference>. We have no reason to think it has any reference to Solomon's marriage with Pharaoh's daughter; if I thought that it had reference to any other than the mystical marriage between Christ and his church, I would rather apply it to some of David's marriages, because he was a man of war, such a one as the bridegroom here is described to be, which Solomon was not. But I take it to be purely and only meant of Jesus Christ; of him speaks the prophet this, of him and of no other man; and to him ( <reference osisRef="Ps.45.6-Ps.45.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>) it is applied in the New Testament (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.8">Heb. i. 8</reference>), nor can it be understood of any other. The preface speaks the excellency of the song, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.1">ver. 1</reference>. The psalm speaks, I. Of the royal bridegroom, who is Christ. 1. The transcendent excellency of his person, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.2">ver. 2</reference>. 2. The glory of his victories, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.3-Ps.45.5">ver. 3-5</reference>. 3. The righteousness of his government, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.6-Ps.45.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>. 4. The splendour of his court, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.8-Ps.45.9">ver. 8, 9</reference>. II. Of the royal bride, which is the church. 1. Her consent gained, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.10-Ps.45.11">ver. 10, 11</reference>. 2. The nuptials solemnized, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.12-Ps.45.15">ver. 12-15</reference>. 3. The issue of this marriage, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.16-Ps.45.17">ver. 16, 17</reference>. In singing this psalm our hearts must be filled with high thoughts of Christ, with an entire submission to and satisfaction in his government, and with an earnest desire of the enlarging and perpetuating of his church in the world.
entries.c628aacb8fc25887800fa9d0dd3574274c9c6eb7: <div eID="gen11210" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11209" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Nuptial Song; Glories of the Messiah.</title> <div sID="gen11211" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> My heart is inditing a good matter: I speak of the things which I have made touching the king: my tongue <hi type="italic">is</hi> the pen of a ready writer. <hi type="super">2</hi> Thou art fairer than the children of men: grace is poured into thy lips: therefore God hath blessed thee for ever. <hi type="super">3</hi> Gird thy sword upon <hi type="italic">thy</hi> thigh, O <hi type="italic">most</hi> mighty, with thy glory and thy majesty. <hi type="super">4</hi> And in thy majesty ride prosperously because of truth and meekness <hi type="italic">and</hi> righteousness; and thy right hand shall teach thee terrible things. <hi type="super">5</hi> Thine arrows <hi type="italic">are</hi> sharp in the heart of the king's enemies; <hi type="italic">whereby</hi> the people fall under thee. <div eID="gen11211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11212" type="x-p"/> Some make <hi type="italic">Shoshannim,</hi> in the title, to signify an instrument of six strings; others take it in its primitive signification for lilies or roses, which probably were strewed, with other flowers, at nuptial solemnities; and then it is easily applicable to Christ who calls himself the <hi type="italic">rose of Sharon and the lily of the valleys,</hi> <reference osisRef="Song.2.1">Cant. ii. 1</reference>. It is <hi type="italic">a song of loves,</hi> concerning the holy love that is between Christ and his church. It is a <hi type="italic">song of the well-beloved,</hi> the virgins, the companions of the bride (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.14">v. 14</reference>), prepared to be sung by them. The virgin-company that attend the Lamb on Mount Zion are said to <hi type="italic">sing a new song,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.14.3-Rev.14.4">Rev. xiv. 3, 4</reference>. <div eID="gen11212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11213" type="x-p"/> I. The preface (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.1">v. 1</reference>) speaks, 1. The dignity of the subject. It is <hi type="italic">a good matter,</hi> and it is a pity that such a moving art as poetry should every be employed about a bad matter. It is <hi type="italic">touching the King,</hi> King Jesus, and his kingdom and government. Note, Those that speak of Christ speak of a good matter, no subject so noble, so copious, so fruitful, so profitable, and so well-becoming us; it is a shame that this good matter is not more the matter of our discourse. 2. The excellency of the management. This song was a confession with the mouth of faith in the heart concerning Christ and his church. (1.) The matter was well digested, as it well deserved: <hi type="italic">My heart is inditing it,</hi> which perhaps is meant of that Spirit of prophecy that dictated the psalm to David, that Spirit of Christ which was in the prophets, <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.11">1 Pet. i. 11</reference>. But it is applicable to his devout meditations and affections in his heart, out of the abundance of which his mouth spoke. Things concerning Christ ought to be thought of by us with all possible seriousness, with fixedness of thought and a fire of holy love, especially when we are to speak of those things. We then speak best of Christ and divine things when we speak from the heart that which has warmed and affected us; and we should never be rash in speaking of the things of Christ, but weigh well beforehand what we have to say, lest we speak amiss. See <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.2">Eccl. v. 2</reference>. (2.) It was well expressed: <hi type="italic">I will speak of the things which I have made.</hi> He would express himself, [1.] With all possible clearness, as one that did himself understand and was affected with the things he spoke of. Not, "I will speak the things I have heard from others," that is speaking by rote; but, "the things which I have myself studied." Note, What God has wrought in our souls, as well as what he has wrought for them, we must declare to others, <reference osisRef="Ps.66.16">Ps. lxvi. 16</reference>. [2.] With all possible cheerfulness, freedom, and fluency: "<hi type="italic">My tongue is</hi> as <hi type="italic">the pen of a ready writer,</hi> guided by my heart in every word as the pen is by the hand." We call the prophets the <hi type="italic">penmen</hi> of scripture, whereas really they were but the pen. The tongue of the most subtle disputant, and the most eloquent orator, is but the pen with which God writes what he pleases. Why should we quarrel with the pen if bitter things be written against us, or idolize the pen if it write in our favour? David not only spoke what he thought of Christ, but wrote it, that it might spread the further and last the longer. His tongue was as the pen of a ready writer, that lets nothing slip. When the heart is inditing a good matter it is a pity but the tongue should be as <hi type="italic">the pen of a ready writer,</hi> to leave it upon record. <div eID="gen11213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11214" type="x-p"/> II. In these verses the Lord Jesus is represented, <div eID="gen11214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11215" type="x-p"/> 1. As most beautiful and amiable in himself. It is a marriage-song; and therefore the transcendent excellencies of Christ are represented by the beauty of the royal bridegroom (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou art fairer than the children of men,</hi> than any of them. He proposed (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.1">v. 1</reference>) to speak of the King, but immediately directs his speech to him. Those that have an admiration and affection for Christ love to go to him and tell him so. Thus we must profess our faith, that we see his beauty, and our love, that we are pleased with it: <hi type="italic">Thou are fair,</hi> thou art <hi type="italic">fairer than the children of men.</hi> Note, Jesus Christ is in himself, and in the eyes of all believers, more amiable and lovely than the children of men. The beauties of the Lord Jesus, as God, as Mediator, far surpass those of human nature in general and those which the most amiable and excellent of the children of men are endowed with; there is more in Christ to engage our love than there is or can be in any creature. Our beloved is more than another beloved. The beauties of this lower world, and its charms, are in danger of drawing away our hearts from Christ, and therefore we are concerned to understand how much he excels them all, and how much more worthy he is of our love. <div eID="gen11215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11216" type="x-p"/> 2. As the great favourite of heaven. He is <hi type="italic">fairer than the children of men,</hi> for God has done more for him than for any of the children of men, and all his kindness to the children of men is for his sake, and passes through his hands, through his mouth. (1.) He has grace, and he has it for us; <hi type="italic">Grace is poured into thy lips.</hi> By his word, his promise, his gospel, the good-will of God is made known to us and the good work of God is begun and carried on in us. He received all grace from God, all the endowments that were requisite to qualify him for his work and office as Mediator, that from his fulness we might receive, <reference osisRef="John.1.16">John i. 16</reference>. It was not only poured into his heart, for his own strength and encouragement, but poured into his lips, that by the words of his mouth in general, and the kisses of his mouth to particular believers, he might communicate both holiness and comfort. From this grace poured into his lips proceeded those gracious words which all admired, <reference osisRef="Luke.4.22">Luke iv. 22</reference>. The gospel of grace is poured into his lips; for it <hi type="italic">began to be spoken by the Lord,</hi> and from him we receive it. He has the words of eternal life. <hi type="italic">The spirit of prophecy is put into thy lips;</hi> so the Chaldee. (2.) He has the blessing, and he has it for us. "Therefore, because thou art the great trustee of divine grace for the use and benefit of the children of men, <hi type="italic">therefore God has blessed thee for ever,</hi> has made thee an everlasting blessing, so as that in thee all the nations of the earth shall be blessed." Where God gives his grace he will give his blessing. We are blessed with spiritual blessings in Christ Jesus, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.3">Eph. i. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen11216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11217" type="x-p"/> 3. As victorious over all his enemies. The royal bridegroom is a man of war, and his nuptials do not excuse him from the field of battle (as was allowed by the law, <reference osisRef="Deut.24.5">Deut. xxiv. 5</reference>); nay, they bring him to the field of battle, for he is to rescue his spouse by dint of sword out of her captivity, to conquer her, and to conquer for her, and then to marry her. Now we have here, <div eID="gen11217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11218" type="x-p"/> (1.) His preparations for war (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Gird thy sword upon thy thigh, O Most Mighty!</hi> The word of God is the sword of the Spirit. By the promises of that word, and the grace contained in those promises, souls are made willing to submit to Jesus Christ and become his loyal subjects; by the threatenings of that word, and the judgments executed according to them, those that stand it out against Christ will, in due time, be brought down and ruined. By the gospel of Christ many Jews and Gentiles were converted, and, at length, the Jewish nation was destroyed, according to the predictions of it, for their implacable enmity to it; and paganism was quite abolished. The sword here girt on Christ's thigh is the same which is said to <hi type="italic">proceed out of his mouth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.19.15">Rev. xix. 15</reference>. When the gospel was sent fort to be preached to all nations, then our Redeemer girded his sword upon his thigh. <div eID="gen11218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11219" type="x-p"/> (2.) His expedition to this holy war: He goes forth <hi type="italic">with his glory and his majesty,</hi> as a great king takes the field with abundance of pomp and magnificence—his sword, his glory, and majesty. In his gospel he appears transcendently great and excellent, bright and blessed, in the honour and majesty which the Father had laid upon him. Christ, both in his person and in his gospel, had nothing of external glory or majesty, nothing to charm men (for he had no form nor comeliness), nothing to awe men, for he <hi type="italic">took upon him the form of a servant;</hi> it was all spiritual glory, spiritual majesty. There is so much grace, and therefore glory, in that word, <hi type="italic">He that believes shall be saved,</hi> so much terror, and therefore majesty, in that word, <hi type="italic">He that believes shall not be damned,</hi> that we may well say, in the chariot of that gospel, which these words are the sum of, the Redeemer rides forth in glory and majesty. <hi type="italic">In thy majesty ride prosperously,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.45.4">v. 4</reference>. <hi type="italic">Prosper thou; ride thou.</hi> This speaks the promise of his Father, that he should prosper according to <hi type="italic">the good pleasure of the Lord,</hi> that he should <hi type="italic">divide the spoil with the strong,</hi> in recompence of his sufferings. Those cannot but prosper to whom God says, Prosper, <reference osisRef="Isa.52.10-Isa.52.12">Isa. lii. 10-12</reference>. And it denotes the good wishes of his friends, praying that he may prosper in the conversion of souls to him, and the destruction of all the powers of darkness that rebel against him. "<hi type="italic">Thy kingdom come;</hi> Go on and prosper." <div eID="gen11219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11220" type="x-p"/> (3.) The glorious cause in which he is engaged—<hi type="italic">because of truth, and meekness, and righteousness,</hi> which were, in a manner, sunk and lost among men, and which Christ came to retrieve and rescue. [1.] The gospel itself is <hi type="italic">truth, meekness, and righteousness;</hi> it commands by the power of truth and righteousness; for Christianity has these, incontestably, on its side, and yet it is to be promoted by meekness and gentleness, <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.12-1Cor.4.13">1 Cor. iv. 12, 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.25">2 Tim. ii. 25</reference>. [2.] Christ appears in it in his <hi type="italic">truth, meekness,</hi> and <hi type="italic">righteousness,</hi> and these are his glory and majesty, and because of these he shall prosper. Men are brought to believe on him because he is true, to learn of him because he is meek, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.29">Matt. xi. 29</reference> (the gentleness of Christ is of mighty force, <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.1">2 Cor. x. 1</reference>), and to submit to him because he is righteous and rules with equity. [3.] The gospel, as far as it prevails with men, sets up in their hearts <hi type="italic">truth, meekness, and righteousness,</hi> rectifies their mistakes by the light of truth, controls their passions by the power of meekness, and governs their hearts and lives by the laws of righteousness. Christ came, by setting up his kingdom among men, to restore those glories to a degenerate world, and to maintain the cause of those just and rightful rulers under him that by error, malice, and iniquity, had been deposed. <div eID="gen11220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11221" type="x-p"/> (4.) The success of his expedition: "<hi type="italic">Thy right hand shall teach thee terrible things;</hi> thou shalt experience a wonderful divine power going along with thy gospel, to make it victorious, and the effects of it will be terrible things." [1.] In order to the conversion and reduction of souls to him, there are terrible things to be done; the heart must be pricked, conscience must be startled, and the terrors of the Lord must make way for his consolations. This is done by the right hand of Christ. The Comforter shall continue, <reference osisRef="John.16.8">John xvi. 8</reference>. [2.] In the conquest of the gates of hell and its supporters, in the destruction of Judaism and Paganism, terrible things will be done, which will make <hi type="italic">men's hearts fail them for fear</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.21.26">Luke xxi. 26</reference>) and great men and chief captains call to the <hi type="italic">rocks and mountains to fall on them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.6.15">Rev. vi. 15</reference>. The next verse describes these terrible things (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thy arrows are sharp in the heart of the king's enemies. First,</hi> Those that were by nature enemies are thus wounded, in order to their being subdued and reconciled. Convictions are like the arrows of the bow, which are sharp in the heart on which they fasten, and bring people to fall under Christ, in subjection to his laws and government. Those that thus fall on this stone shall by broken, <reference osisRef="Matt.21.44">Matt. xxi. 44</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Those that persist in their enmity are thus wounded, in order to their being ruined. The arrows of God's terrors are sharp in their hearts, whereby they shall fall under him, so as to be made his footstool, <reference osisRef="Ps.110.1">Ps. cx. 1</reference>. Those that would not have him to reign over them shall be brought forth and slain before him (<reference osisRef="Luke.19.27">Luke xix. 27</reference>); those that would not submit to his golden sceptre shall be broken to pieces by his iron rod.
entries.3ca5a8ce5a0acff7f6715fab5f7ba8650d4e0df7: <div eID="gen11221" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Majesty and Glory of Christ.</title> <div sID="gen11222" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Thy throne, O God, <hi type="italic">is</hi> for ever and ever: the sceptre of thy kingdom <hi type="italic">is</hi> a right sceptre. <hi type="super">7</hi> Thou lovest righteousness, and hatest wickedness: therefore God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows. <hi type="super">8</hi> All thy garments <hi type="italic">smell</hi> of myrrh, and aloes, <hi type="italic">and</hi> cassia, out of the ivory palaces, whereby they have made thee glad. <hi type="super">9</hi> Kings' daughters <hi type="italic">were</hi> among thy honourable women: upon thy right hand did stand the queen in gold of Ophir. <div eID="gen11222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11223" type="x-p"/> We have here the royal bridegroom filling his throne with judgment and keeping his court with splendour. <div eID="gen11223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11224" type="x-p"/> I. He here fills his throne with judgment. It is God the Father that says to the Son here, <hi type="italic">Thy throne, O God! is forever and ever,</hi> as appears <reference osisRef="Heb.1.8-Heb.1.9">Heb. i. 8, 9</reference>, where this is quoted to prove that he is God and has a <hi type="italic">more excellent name than the angels.</hi> The Mediator is God, else he neither would have been able to do the Mediator's work nor fit to wear the Mediator's crown. Concerning his government observe, 1. The eternity of it; it is <hi type="italic">for ever and ever.</hi> It shall continue on earth throughout all the ages of time, in despite of all the opposition of the gates of hell; and in the blessed fruits and consequences of it it shall last as long as the days of heaven, and run parallel with the line of eternity itself. Perhaps even then the glory of the Redeemer, and the blessedness of the redeemed, shall be in a continual infinite progression; for it is promised that not only of his government, but of <hi type="italic">the increase of his government and peace, there shall be no end</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.7">Isa. ix. 7</reference>); even when the kingdom shall be <hi type="italic">delivered up to God even the Father</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.24">1 Cor. xv. 24</reference>) the throne of the Redeemer will continue. 2. The equity of it: <hi type="italic">The sceptre of thy kingdom,</hi> the administration of thy government, <hi type="italic">is right,</hi> exactly according to the eternal counsel and will of God, which is the eternal rule and reason of good and evil. Whatever Christ does he does none of his subjects any wrong, but gives redress to those that do suffer wrong: <hi type="italic">He loves righteousness, and hates wickedness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.45.7">v. 7</reference>. He himself loves to do righteousness, and hates to do wickedness; and he loves those that do righteousness, and hates those that do wickedness. By the holiness of his life, the merit of his death, and the great design of his gospel, he has made it to appear that he loves righteousness (for by his example, his satisfaction, and his precepts, he has brought in an everlasting righteousness), and that he hates wickedness, for never did God's hatred of sin appear so conspicuously as it did in the sufferings of Christ. 3. The establishment and elevation of it: <hi type="italic">Therefore God, even thy God</hi> (Christ, as Mediator, called God <hi type="italic">his God,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.20.17">John xx. 17</reference>, as commissioned by him, and the head of those that are taken into covenant with him), <hi type="italic">has anointed thee with the oil of gladness. Therefore,</hi> that is, (1.) "In order to this righteous government of thine, God has given thee his Spirit, that divine unction, to qualify thee for thy undertaking," <reference osisRef="Isa.61.1">Isa. lxi. 1</reference>. 1. <hi type="italic">The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because he has anointed me.</hi> What God called him to he fitted him for, <reference osisRef="Isa.11.2">Isa. xi. 2</reference>. The Spirit is called <hi type="italic">the oil of gladness</hi> because of the delight wherewith Christ was filled in carrying on his undertaking. He was anointed with the Spirit <hi type="italic">above all his fellows,</hi> above all those that were anointed, whether priests or kings. (2.) "In recompence of what thou has done and suffered for the advancement of righteousness and the destruction of sin God has anointed thee with the oil of gladness, has brought thee to all the honours and all the joys of thy exalted state." <hi type="italic">Because he humbled himself, God has highly exalted him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.2.8-Phil.2.9">Phil. ii. 8, 9</reference>. His anointing him denotes the power and glory to which he is exalted; he is invested in all the dignities and authorities of the Messiah. And his anointing him with the oil of gladness denotes <hi type="italic">the joy that was set before him</hi> (so his exaltation is expressed, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.2">Heb. xii. 2</reference>) both in the light of his <hi type="italic">Father's countenance</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.28">Acts ii. 28</reference>) and in the success of his undertaking, which he shall <hi type="italic">see, and be satisfied,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.53.11">Isa. liii. 11</reference>. This he is anointed with <hi type="italic">above all his fellows,</hi> above all believers, who are his brethren, and who partake of the anointing—they by measure, he without measure. But the apostle brings it to prove his pre-eminence above the angels, <reference osisRef="Heb.1.4">Heb. i. 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.1.9">9</reference>. The salvation of sinners is the joy of angels (<reference osisRef="Luke.15.10">Luke xv. 10</reference>), but much more of the Son. <div eID="gen11224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11225" type="x-p"/> II. He keeps his court with splendour and magnificence. 1. His robes of state, wherein he appears, are taken notice of, not for their pomp, which might strike an awe upon the spectator, but their pleasantness and the gratefulness of the odours with which they were perfumed (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">They smell of myrrh, aloes, and cassia</hi> (the <hi type="italic">oil of gladness</hi> with which he and his garments were anointed): these were some of the ingredients of the holy anointing oil which God appointed, the like to which was not to be made up for any common use (<reference osisRef="Exod.30.23-Exod.30.24">Exod. xxx. 23, 24</reference>), which was typical of the unction of the Spirit which Christ, the great high priest of our profession, received, and to which therefore there seems here to be a reference. It is the savour of these good ointments, his graces and comforts, that draws souls to him (<reference osisRef="Song.1.3-Song.1.4">Cant. i. 3, 4</reference>) and makes him <hi type="italic">precious to believers,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.7">1 Pet. ii. 7</reference>. 2. His royal palaces are said to be <hi type="italic">ivory</hi> ones, such as were then reckoned most magnificent. We read of an ivory house that Ahab made, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.39">1 Kings xxii. 39</reference>. The mansions of light above are the <hi type="italic">ivory palaces,</hi> whence all the joys both of Christ and believers come, and where they will be for ever in perfection; for by them he is made glad, and all that are his with him; for they shall enter into the joy of their Lord. 3. The beauties of his court shine very brightly. In public appearances at court, when the pomp of it is shown, nothing is supposed to contribute so much to it as the splendour of the ladies, which is alluded to here, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.9">v. 9</reference>. (1.) Particular believers are here compared to the ladies at court, richly dressed in honour of the sovereign: <hi type="italic">Kings' daughters are among thy honourable women,</hi> whose looks, and mien, and ornaments, we may suppose, from the height of their extraction, to excel all others. All true believers are born from above; they are the children of the King of kings. These attend the throne of the Lord Jesus daily with their prayers and praises, which is really their honour, and he is pleased to reckon it his. The numbering of kings' daughters among his honourable women, or maids of honour, intimates that the kings whose daughters they were should be tributaries to him and dependents on him, and would therefore think it a preferment to their daughters to attend him. (2.) The church in general, constituted of these particular believers, is here compared to the queen herself—the queen-consort, whom, by an everlasting covenant, he hath betrothed to himself. She stands <hi type="italic">at his right hand,</hi> near to him, and receives honour from him, in the richest array, <hi type="italic">in gold of Ophir,</hi> in robes woven with golden thread or with a gold chain and other ornaments of gold. This is <hi type="italic">the bride, the Lamb's wife,</hi> whose graces, which are her ornaments, are compared to <hi type="italic">fine linen, clean and white</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.8">Rev. xix. 8</reference>), for their purity, here to <hi type="italic">gold of Ophir,</hi> for their costliness; for, as we owe our redemption, so we owe our adorning, not to corruptible things, but to <hi type="italic">the precious blood of the Son of God.</hi>
entries.afa4cd93a85d041da24bf3d97d52610e993d1b57: <div eID="gen11225" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Glory of the Church.</title> <div sID="gen11226" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> Hearken, O daughter, and consider, and incline thine ear; forget also thine own people, and thy father's house; <hi type="super">11</hi> So shall the king greatly desire thy beauty: for he <hi type="italic">is</hi> thy Lord; and worship thou him. <hi type="super">12</hi> And the daughter of Tyre <hi type="italic">shall be there</hi> with a gift; <hi type="italic">even</hi> the rich among the people shall intreat thy favour. <hi type="super">13</hi> The king's daughter <hi type="italic">is</hi> all glorious within: her clothing <hi type="italic">is</hi> of wrought gold. <hi type="super">14</hi> She shall be brought unto the king in raiment of needlework: the virgins her companions that follow her shall be brought unto thee. <hi type="super">15</hi> With gladness and rejoicing shall they be brought: they shall enter into the king's palace. <hi type="super">16</hi> Instead of thy fathers shall be thy children, whom thou mayest make princes in all the earth. <hi type="super">17</hi> I will make thy name to be remembered in all generations: therefore shall the people praise thee for ever and ever. <div eID="gen11226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11227" type="x-p"/> This latter part of the psalm is addressed to the royal bride, standing on the right hand of the royal bridegroom. God, who said to the Son, <hi type="italic">Thy throne is for ever and ever,</hi> says this to the church, which, upon the account of her espousals to the Son, he here calls his <hi type="italic">daughter.</hi> <div eID="gen11227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11228" type="x-p"/> I. He tells her of the duties expected from her, which ought to be considered by all those that come into relation to the Lord Jesus: "<hi type="italic">Hearken,</hi> therefore, <hi type="italic">and consider</hi> this, <hi type="italic">and incline thy ear,</hi> that is, submit to those conditions of thy espousals, and bring thy will to comply with them." This is the method of profiting by the word of God. <hi type="italic">He that has ears, let him hear,</hi> let him hearken diligently; he that hearkens, let him consider and weigh it duly; he that considers, let him incline and yield to the force of what is laid before him. And what is it that is here required? <div eID="gen11228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11229" type="x-p"/> 1. She must renounce all others. <div eID="gen11229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11230" type="x-p"/> (1.) Here is the law of her espousals: "<hi type="italic">Forget thy own people and thy father's house,</hi> according to the law of marriage. Retain not the affection thou hast had for them, nor covet to return to them again; banish all such remembrance (not only of thy people that were dear to thee, but of thy father's house that were dearer) as may incline thee to look back, as Lot's wife to Sodom." When Abraham, in obedience to God's call, had quitted his native soil, he was not so much as <hi type="italic">mindful of the country whence he came out.</hi> This shows, [1.] How necessary it was for those who were converted from Judaism or paganism to the faith of Christ wholly to cast out the old leaven, and not to bring into their Christian profession either the Jewish ceremonies or the heathen idolatries, for these would make such a mongrel religion in Christianity as the Samaritans had. [2.] How necessary it is for us all, when we give up our names to Jesus Christ, to hate father and mother, and all that is dear to us in this world, in comparison, that is, to love them less than Christ and his honour, and our interest in him, <reference osisRef="Luke.14.26">Luke xiv. 26</reference>. <div eID="gen11230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11231" type="x-p"/> (2.) Here is good encouragement given to the royal bride thus entirely to break off from her former alliances: <hi type="italic">So shall the king greatly desire thy beauty,</hi> which intimates that the mixing of her old rites and customs, whether Jewish or Gentile, with her religion, would blemish her beauty and would hazard her interest in the affections of the royal bridegroom, but that, if she entirely conformed to his will, he would delight in her. The beauty of holiness, both on the church and on particular believers, is in the sight of Christ of great price and very amiable. Where that is he says, <hi type="italic">This is my rest for ever; here will I dwell, for I have desired it.</hi> Among the golden candlesticks he walks with pleasure, <reference osisRef="Rev.2.1">Rev. ii. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen11231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11232" type="x-p"/> 2. She must reverence him, must love, honour, and obey him: <hi type="italic">He is thy Lord, and worship thou him.</hi> The church is to be subject to Christ as the wife to the husband (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.24">Eph. v. 24</reference>), to call him <hi type="italic">Lord,</hi> as Sarah called Abraham, and to obey him (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.6">1 Pet. iii. 6</reference>), and so not only to submit to his government, but to give him divine honours. We must worship him as God, and our Lord; for this is the will of God, that <hi type="italic">all men should honour the Son even as they honour the Father;</hi> nay, in so doing it is reckoned that they honour the Father. If we confess that Christ is Lord, and pay our homage to him accordingly, it is <hi type="italic">to the glory of God the Father,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.2.11">Phil. ii. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen11232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11233" type="x-p"/> II. He tells her of the honours designed for her. <div eID="gen11233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11234" type="x-p"/> 1. Great court should be made to her, and rich presents brought her (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.12">v. 12</reference>): "<hi type="italic">The daughter of Tyre,</hi>" a rich and splendid city, "the <hi type="italic">daughter of the King of Tyre</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">there with a gift;</hi> every royal family round about shall send a branch, as a representative of the whole, to seek thy favour and to make an interest in thee; <hi type="italic">even the rich among the people,</hi> whose wealth might be thought to exempt them from dependence at court, even they shall entreat thy favour, for his sake to whom thou art espoused, that by thee they may make him their friend." The Jews, the pretending Jews, who are rich to a proverb (as rich as a Jew), shall come and worship before the church's feet in the Philadelphian period, and shall <hi type="italic">know that Christ has loved her,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.3.9">Rev. iii. 9</reference>. When the Gentiles, being converted to the faith of Christ, join themselves to the church, they then <hi type="italic">come with a gift,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.5">2 Cor. viii. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.15.16">Rom. xv. 16</reference>. When with themselves they devote all they have to the honour of Christ, and the service of his kingdom, they then <hi type="italic">come with a gift.</hi> <div eID="gen11234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11235" type="x-p"/> 2. She shall be very splendid, and highly esteemed in the eyes of all, (1.) For her personal qualifications, the endowments of her mind, which every one shall admire (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">The king's daughter is all glorious within.</hi> Note, The glory of the church is spiritual glory, and that is indeed all glory; it is the glory of the soul, and that is the man; it is glory in God's sight, and it is an earnest of eternal glory. The glory of the saints falls not within the view of a carnal eye. As their life, so their glory, is hidden with Christ in God, neither can the natural man know it, for it is spiritually discerned; but those who do so discern it highly value it. Let us see here what is that true glory which we should be ambitious of, not that which <hi type="italic">makes a fair show in the flesh,</hi> but which is in <hi type="italic">the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.4">1 Pet. iii. 4</reference>), <hi type="italic">whose praise is not of men, but of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.2.29">Rom. ii. 29</reference>. (2.) For her rich apparel. Though all her glory is within, that for which she is truly valuable, yet <hi type="italic">her clothing</hi> also <hi type="italic">is of wrought gold;</hi> the conversation of Christians, in which they appear in the world, must be enriched with good works, not gay and gaudy ones, like paint and flourish, but substantially good, like gold; and it must be accurate and exact, like wrought gold, which is worked with a great deal of care and caution. <div eID="gen11235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11236" type="x-p"/> 3. Her nuptials shall be celebrated with a great deal of honour and joy (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.14-Ps.45.15">v. 14, 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">She shall be brought to the king,</hi> as the Lord God brought the woman to the man (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.22">Gen. ii. 22</reference>), which was a type of this mystical marriage between Christ and his church. None are brought to Christ but whom the Father brings, and he has undertaken to do it; none besides are so brought <hi type="italic">to the king</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.14">v. 14</reference>) as to <hi type="italic">enter into the king's palace,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.45.15">v. 15</reference>. <div eID="gen11236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11237" type="x-p"/> (1.) This intimates a two-fold bringing of the spouse to Christ. [1.] In the conversion of souls to Christ; then they are espoused to him, privately contracted, as chaste virgins, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.2">2 Cor. xi. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.7.4">Rom. vii. 4</reference>. [2.] In the completing of the mystical body, and the glorification of all the saints, at the end of time; then the <hi type="italic">bride, the Lamb's wife,</hi> shall be made completely ready, when all that belong to the election of grace shall be called in and called home, and all gathered together to Christ, <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.1">2 Thess. ii. 1</reference>. Then is the marriage of the Lamb come (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.7">Rev. xix. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.2">xxi. 2</reference>), and the virgins <hi type="italic">go forth to meet the bridegroom,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.25.1">Matt. xxv. 1</reference>. Then they shall <hi type="italic">enter into the king's palaces,</hi> into the heavenly mansions, to be ever with the Lord. <div eID="gen11237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11238" type="x-p"/> (2.) In both these espousals, observe, to the honour of the royal bride, [1.] Her wedding clothes—<hi type="italic">raiment of needle-work,</hi> the righteousness of Christ, the graces of the Spirit; both curiously wrought by divine wisdom. [2.] Her bride-maids—<hi type="italic">the virgins her companions,</hi> the wise virgins who have oil in their vessels as well as in their lamps, those who, being joined to the church, cleave to it and follow it, these shall go in to the marriage. [3.] The mirth with which the nuptials will be celebrated: <hi type="italic">With gladness and rejoicing shall she be brought.</hi> When the prodigal is brought home to his father <hi type="italic">it is meet that we should make merry and be glad</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.15.32">Luke xv. 32</reference>); and when the marriage of the Lamb has come <hi type="italic">let us be glad and rejoice</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.7">Rev. xix. 7</reference>); for the <hi type="italic">day of his espousals is the day of the gladness of his heart,</hi> <reference osisRef="Song.3.11">Cant. iii. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen11238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11239" type="x-p"/> 4. The progeny of this marriage shall be illustrious (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">Instead of thy fathers shall be thy children.</hi> Instead of the Old-Testament church, the economy of which had waxed old, and ready to <hi type="italic">vanish away</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.8.13">Heb. viii. 13</reference>), as the fathers that are going off, there shall be a New-Testament church, a Gentile-church, that shall be grafted into the same olive and partake of its <hi type="italic">root and fatness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.17">Rom. xi. 17</reference>); more and more eminent shall be <hi type="italic">the children of the desolate</hi> than <hi type="italic">the children of the married wife,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.54.1">Isa. liv. 1</reference>. This promise to Christ is of the same import with that <reference osisRef="Isa.53.10">Isa. liii. 10</reference>, <hi type="italic">He shall see his seed;</hi> and these shall be made <hi type="italic">princes in all the earth;</hi> there shall be some of all nations brought into subjection to Christ, and so made princes, <hi type="italic">made to our God kings and priests,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.1.6">Rev. i. 6</reference>. Or it may intimate that there should be a much greater number of Christian kings than ever there was of Jewish kings (those in Canaan only, these in all the earth), nursing fathers and nursing mothers to the church, which shall <hi type="italic">suck the breasts of kings.</hi> They are princes of Christ's making; for <hi type="italic">by him kings reign and princes decree justice.</hi> <div eID="gen11239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11240" type="x-p"/> 5. The praise of this marriage shall be perpetual in the praises of the royal bridegroom (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will make thy name to be remembered.</hi> His Father has given him <hi type="italic">a name above every name,</hi> and here promises to make it perpetual, by keeping up a succession of ministers and Christians in every age, that shall bear up his name, which shall thus <hi type="italic">endure for ever</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.17">Ps. lxxii. 17</reference>), by being remembered in all the generations of time; for the entail of Christianity shall not be cut off. "Therefore, because they shall remember thee in all generations, they shall praise thee for ever and ever." Those that help to support the honour of Christ on earth shall in heaven see his glory, and share in it, and be for ever praising him. In the believing hope of our everlasting happiness in the other world let us always keep up the remembrance of Christ, as our only way thither, in our generation; and, in assurance of the perpetuating of the kingdom of the Redeemer in the world, let us transmit the remembrance of him to succeeding generations, that his name <hi type="italic">may endure for ever and be as the days of heaven.</hi>  <chapter eID="Ps.45"/> <div eID="gen11240" type="x-p"/>

entries.1dacb1c5b1f1573e9a51b35f2737a175836a0e17: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5984"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 45</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.45.1-Ps.45.17">Psa 45:1-17</reference>. Shoshannim--literally, "Lilies," either descriptive of an instrument so shaped, or denoting some tune or air so called, after which the Psalm was to be sung (see on <reference osisRef="Ps.8.1">Psa 8:1</reference>, title). A song of loves, or, of beloved ones (plural and feminine)--a conjugal song. Maschil--(See on <reference osisRef="Ps.32.1">Psa 32:1</reference>, title, and <reference osisRef="Ps.42.1">Psa 42:1</reference>, title) denotes the didactic character of the Psalm; that it gives instruction, the song being of allegorical, and not literal, import. The union and glories of Christ and his Church are described. He is addressed as a king possessed of all essential graces, as a conqueror exalted on the throne of a righteous and eternal government, and as a bridegroom arrayed in nuptial splendor. The Church is portrayed in the purity and loveliness of a royally adorned and attended bride, invited to forsake her home and share the honors of her affianced lord. The picture of an Oriental wedding thus opened is filled up by representing the complimentary gifts of the wealthy with which the occasion is honored, the procession of the bride clothed in splendid raiment, attended by her virgin companions, and the entrance of the joyous throng into the palace of the king. A prediction of a numerous and distinguished progeny, instead of the complimentary wish for it usually expressed (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.24.60">Ge 24:60</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ruth.4.11">Ru 4:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ruth.4.12">12</reference>), and an assurance of a perpetual fame, closes the Psalm. All ancient Jewish and Christian interpreters regarded this Psalm as an allegory of the purport above named. In the Song of Songs the allegory is carried out more fully. Hosea (Ho 1:<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.5">1-3:5</reference>) treats the relation of God and His people under the same figure, and its use to set forth the relation of Christ and His Church runs through both parts of the Bible (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.54.5">Is 54:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.62.4">62:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.62.5">5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.22.3">Mt 22:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.25.1">25:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.3.29">Joh 3:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.25-Eph.5.32">Ep 5:25-32</reference>, &c.). Other methods of exposition have been suggested. Several Jewish monarchs, from Solomon to the wicked Ahab, and various foreign princes, have been named as the hero of the song. But to none of them can the terms here used be shown to apply, and it is hardly probable that any mere nuptial song, especially of a heathen king, would be permitted a place in the sacred songs of the Jews. The advocates for any other than the Messianic interpretation have generally silenced each other in succession, while the application of the most rigorous rules of a fair system of interpretation has but strengthened the evidences in its favor. The scope of the Psalm above given is easy and sustained by the explication of its details. The quotation of <reference osisRef="Ps.45.6">Psa 45:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.7">7</reference> by Paul (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.8">He 1:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.9">9</reference>), as applicable to Christ, ought to be conclusive, and their special exposition shows the propriety of such an application.</title> <div sID="gen9108" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5984"/>1. An animated preface indicative of strong emotion. Literally, "My heart overflows: a good matter I speak; the things which I have made," &c.<div eID="gen9108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9109" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">inditing--</hi>literally, "boiling up," as a fountain overflows.<div eID="gen9109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9110" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my tongue is the pen--</hi>a mere instrument of God's use.<div eID="gen9110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9111" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of a ready writer--</hi>that is, it is fluent. The theme is inspiring and language flows fast. <div eID="gen9111" type="x-p"/>
entries.49ac58fa345e78744915b5573ac679c45766a821: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5985"/><div sID="gen9112" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5985"/>2. To rich personal attractions is added grace of the lips, captivating powers of speech. This is given, and becomes a source of power and proves a blessing. Christ is a prophet (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.22">Lu 4:22</reference>). <div eID="gen9112" type="x-p"/>
entries.603fa2f9da333e00809d39e90a164694c83ba083: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5986"/><div sID="gen9113" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5986"/>3-4. The king is addressed as ready to go forth to battle.<div eID="gen9113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9114" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sword--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Rev.1.16">Re 1:16</reference>; 19:15).<div eID="gen9114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9115" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mighty--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Is 9:6</reference>).<div eID="gen9115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9116" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">glory and ... majesty--</hi>generally used as divine attributes (<reference osisRef="Ps.96.6">Psa 96:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.104.1">104:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.111.3">111:3</reference>), or as specially conferred on mortals (<reference osisRef="Ps.21.5">Psa 21:5</reference>), perhaps these typically. <div eID="gen9116" type="x-p"/>
entries.fe8ffd1cc4074cf9b434efab80fdbb7fc0b1e7bd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5988"/><div sID="gen9122" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5988"/>5. The result.<div eID="gen9122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9123" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">people--</hi>Whole nations are subdued. <div eID="gen9123" type="x-p"/>
entries.ccf9b6041c43d9a6bb407d4565092e4631eb5087: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5989"/><div sID="gen9124" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5989"/>6. No lawful construction can be devised to change the sense here given and sustained by the ancient versions, and above all by Paul (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.8">He 1:8</reference>). Of the perpetuity of this government, compare <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.13">2Sa 7:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.10.16">Psa 10:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.72.5">72:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.89.4">89:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.110.4">110:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.9.7">Is 9:7</reference>. <div eID="gen9124" type="x-p"/>
entries.07ef7796c2d3ac933331e3abdc652de64e29dc7f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5990"/><div sID="gen9125" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5990"/>7. As in <reference osisRef="Ps.45.6">Psa 45:6</reference> the divine nature is made prominent, here the moral qualities of the human are alleged as the reason or ground of the mediatorial exultation. Some render "O God, thy God," instead of<div eID="gen9125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9126" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">God, thy God--</hi>but the latter is sustained by the same form (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.7">Psa 50:7</reference>), and it was only of His human nature that the anointing could be predicated (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.61.3">Is 61:3</reference>).<div eID="gen9126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9127" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">oil of gladness--</hi>or token of gladness, as used in feasts and other times of solemn joy (compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.1.39">1Ki 1:39</reference>, 40).<div eID="gen9127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9128" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fellows--</hi>other kings. <div eID="gen9128" type="x-p"/>
entries.868de262e85d611f01992560cc9cea14545eb634: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5991"/><div sID="gen9129" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5991"/>8. The king thus inaugurated is now presented as a bridegroom, who appears in garments richly perfumed, brought out from<div eID="gen9129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9130" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ivory palaces--</hi>His royal residence; by which, as indications of the happy bridal occasion, He has been gladdened. <div eID="gen9130" type="x-p"/>
entries.5c9e1a8c2f4617b5fb091fccbbe7bcd2faea58c0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5992"/><div sID="gen9131" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5992"/>9. In completion of this picture of a marriage festival, female attendants or bridesmaids of the highest rank attend Him, while the queen, in rich apparel (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.13">Psa 45:13</reference>), stands ready for the nuptial procession. <div eID="gen9131" type="x-p"/>
entries.41f338418160bdeae9d8b2901b95bc85fb617a55: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5993"/><div sID="gen9132" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5993"/>10-11. She is invited to the union, for forming which she must leave her father's people. She representing, by the form of the allegory, the Church, this address is illustrated by all those scriptures, from <reference osisRef="Gen.12.1">Ge 12:1</reference> on, which speak of the people of God as a chosen, separate, and peculiar people. The relation of subjection to her spouse at once accords with the law of marriage, as given in <reference osisRef="Gen.3.16">Ge 3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.18.12">18:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.22">Ep 5:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.5">1Pe 3:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.6">6</reference>, and the relation of the Church to Christ (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.24">Ep 5:24</reference>). The love of the husband is intimately connected with the entire devotion to which the bride is exhorted. <div eID="gen9132" type="x-p"/>
entries.bafe5d22135f6a01e6b394cde47360c276369ab3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5994"/><div sID="gen9133" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5994"/><hi type="bold">12. daughter of Tyre--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.9.14">Psa 9:14</reference>); denotes the people. Tyre, celebrated for its great wealth, is selected to represent the richest nations, an idea confirmed by the next clause. These gifts are brought as means to conciliate the royal parties, representing the admitted subjection of the offerers. This well sets forth the exalted position of the Church and her head, whose moral qualities receive the homage of the world. The contribution of material wealth to sustain the institutions of the Church may be included (compare "riches of the Gentiles," <reference osisRef="Ps.72.10">Psa 72:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.60.5-Isa.60.10">Is 60:5-10</reference>). <div eID="gen9133" type="x-p"/>
entries.d46c923498faadabacd5e57ded139002f01dd720: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5995"/><div sID="gen9134" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5995"/><hi type="bold">13. the king's daughter--</hi>a term of dignity. It may also intimate, with some allusion to the teaching of the allegory, that the bride of Christ, the Church, is the daughter of the great king, God.<div eID="gen9134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9135" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">within--</hi>Not only is her outward raiment costly, but all her apparel is of the richest texture.<div eID="gen9135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9136" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wrought gold--</hi>gold embroidery, or cloth in which gold is woven. <div eID="gen9136" type="x-p"/>
entries.b4b2bc1000c508f3308d74c85f8c63b5604dd04a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5996"/><div sID="gen9137" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5996"/> <hi type="bold">14-15. The progress of the procession is described; according to the usual custom the bride and attendants are conducted to the palace. Some for the words--</hi> <div eID="gen9137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9138" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in raiment of needlework--</hi>propose another rendering, "on variegated (or embroidered) cloths"--that is, in the manner of the East, richly wrought tapestry was spread on the ground, on which the bride walked. As the dress had been already mentioned, this seems to be a probable translation. <div eID="gen9138" type="x-p"/>
entries.9c1e547d5e14b8e0268027579f48a5f28299bb7a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5998"/><div sID="gen9140" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5998"/>16. As earthly monarchs govern widely extended empires by viceroys, this glorious king is represented as supplying all the principalities of earth with princes of his own numerous progeny. <div eID="gen9140" type="x-p"/>
entries.d5979c2975035b6ab706e47daa11cc85fc9ac45e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5999"/><div sID="gen9141" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5999"/>17. The glories of this empire shall be as wide as the world and lasting as eternity.<div eID="gen9141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9142" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">therefore--</hi>Because thus glorious, the praise shall be universal and perpetual. Some writers have taxed their ingenuity to find in the history and fortunes of Christ and His Church exact parallels for every part of this splendid allegory, not excepting its gorgeous Oriental imagery. Thus, by the dresses of the king and queen, are thought to be meant the eminent endowments and graces of Christ and His people. The attendant women, supposed (though inconsistently it might seem with the inspired character of the work) to be concubines, are thought to represent the Gentile churches, and the bride the Jewish, &c. But it is evident that we cannot pursue such a mode of interpretation. For, following the allegory, we must suspend to the distant future the results of a union whose consummation as a marriage is still distant (compare <reference osisRef="Rev.21.9">Re 21:9</reference>). In fact, the imagery here and elsewhere sets before us the Church in two aspects. As a body, it is yet incomplete, the whole is yet ungathered. As a moral institution, it is yet imperfect. In the final catastrophe it will be complete and perfect. Thus, as a bride adorned, &c., it will be united with its Lord. Thus the union of Christ and the Church triumphant is set forth. On the other hand, in regard to its component parts, the relation of Christ as head, as husband, &c., already exists, and as these parts form an institution in this world, it is by His union with it, and the gifts and graces with which He endows it, that a spiritual seed arises and spreads in the world. Hence we must fix our minds only on the one simple but grand truth, that Christ loves the Church, is head over all things for it, raises it in His exaltation to the highest moral dignity--a dignity of which every, even the meanest, sincere disciple will partake. As to the time, then, in which this allegorical prophecy is to fulfilled, it may be said that no periods of time are specially designated. The characteristics of the relation of Christ and His Church are indicated, and we may suppose that the whole process of His exaltation from the declaration of His Sonship, by His resurrection, to the grand catastrophe of the final judgment, with all the collateral blessings to the Church and the world, lay before the vision of the inspired prophet. <chapter eID="Ps.45"/>

entries.d6e4abf1cf5fefc9546855046717ed9b79322fda: <div eID="gen20060" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen20061" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20062" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20062" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20061" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20063" type="x-p"/> The contents of this Psalm are generally summed up thus: The majesty and grace of Christ's kingdom; or an epithalamium of Jesus Christ and the Christian Church; the duty of this Church, and its privileges. The Psalm contains a magnificent description of the beauty, ornaments, valor, justice, and truth of the Divine Bridegroom; the beauty, magnificence, and riches of the bride, who was to become mother of a numerous and powerful posterity. The preamble is found in the title and <reference osisRef="Psa.45.1">Psa 45:1</reference>. The description and character of the Bridegroom, <reference osisRef="Psa.45.2-Psa.45.9">Psa 45:2-9</reference>. The address to the bride by her companions, <reference osisRef="Psa.45.10-Psa.45.15">Psa 45:10-15</reference>. A prediction of her numerous and glorious descendants, <reference osisRef="Psa.45.16">Psa 45:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.45.17">Psa 45:17</reference>. <div eID="gen20063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20064" type="x-p"/> The title is nearly the same with that of Psalm 69: and 80: "To the chief musician, or master of the band of those who played on the six-stringed instruments, giving instruction for the sons of Korah; a song of loves, or amatory ode; or a song of the beloved maids." The Vulgate and Septuagint have, For those who shall be changed, or brought into another state, which some have interpreted as relating to the resurrection of the just, but if I could persuade myself that the title came by Divine inspiration, I would say it more properly belonged to the calling and conversion of the Gentiles, and bringing them over from idolatry to the worship of the true God. By some the word ששנים shoshannim, is translated lilies; and a world of labor has been spent to prove that these lilies mean the saints, Jesus Christ himself, and the Divine light which is a banner to them that fear him. I cannot believe that any such meaning is intended, and, consequently, I cannot attempt to interpret the Psalm after this model. I believe it to be an epithalamium, or nuptial song, which primarily respected Solomon's marriage with the daughter of Pharaoh; and that it probably has a prophetic reference to the conversion of the Gentiles, and the final aggrandizement of the Christian Church. <div eID="gen20064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20065" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen20065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20066" type="x-p"/> My heart is inditing a good matter - רחש rachash, boileth or bubbleth up, as in the margin. It is a metaphor taken from a fountain that sends up its waters from the earth in this way. The Vulgate has eructavit, which is most literally translated by the old Psalter: Mi hert ryfted gude word. My heart belcheth - Anglo-Saxon. <div eID="gen20066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20067" type="x-p"/> I speak of the things which I have made touching the king - אמר אני מעשי למלך, literally, "I dedicate my work unto the king." Or, as the Psalter, I say my werkes til the kyng. This was the general custom of the Asiatic poets. They repeated their works before princes and honorable men; and especially those parts in which there was either a direct or constructive compliment to the great man. Virgil is reported to have a part of his Aeneid before Augustus, who was so pleased with it that he ordered ten sestertia to be given him for every line. And the famous Persian poet Ferdusi read a part of his Shah Nameh before Sultan Mahmoud, who promised him thirty thousand denars for the poem. <div eID="gen20067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20068" type="x-p"/> My tongue is the pen of a ready writer - I shall compose and speak as fluently the Divine matter which is now in my heart, as the most expert scribe can write from my recitation. My tung of maister swiftly wrytand. "That es, my tung is pen of the Haly Gast; and nout but als his instrument, wham he ledis als he wil. For I speke noght bot that he settis on my tung; als the pen dos noght withouten the writer. Swyftly wrytand, for the vertu of goddes inspiracioun is noght for to thynk with mons study, that he schewes til other of the purete of heven; that es some for to com that he wrytes." - Old Psalter.
entries.8290145482ad4f243a0c6634e80466fcb7d3d3f3: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen20068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20069" type="x-p"/> Thou art fairer than the children of men - By whom are these words spoken? As this is a regular epithalamium, we are to consider that the bride and bridegroom have compliments paid them by those called the friends of the bridegroom, and the companions or maids of the bride. But it seems that the whole Psalm, except the first verse, was spoken by those who are called in the title ידידת yedidoth, the beloved maids, or female companions, who begin with his perfections, and then describe hers. And afterwards there is a prophetical declaration concerning his issue. We may, therefore, consider that what is spoken here is spoken by companions of the bride, or what are called yedidoth in the title. It would be unauthenticated to say Solomon was the most beautiful man in the universe; but to the perfections of the Lord Jesus they may be safely applied. <div eID="gen20069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20070" type="x-p"/> Grace is poured into thy lips - This probably refers to his speech, or the gracious words which he spoke. Solomon was renowned for wisdom, and especially the wisdom of his conversation. The queen of Sheba came from the uttermost parts of the land to hear the wisdom of Solomon; and so far did she find him exceeding all his fame, that she said one half had not been told her: but behold, a greater than Solomon is here. No man ever spoke like this man, his enemies themselves being judges. <div eID="gen20070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20071" type="x-p"/> God hath blessed thee for ever - This, I am afraid, could in no sense be ever spoken of Solomon; but of the man Christ Jesus it is strictly true.
entries.c288629af1c7a390ea2e15e9d1f8234538620200: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen20071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20072" type="x-p"/> Gird thy sword upon thy thigh, O most mighty - This clause should be translated, O hero, gird thy sword upon thy thigh! This, I think, cannot be spoken of Solomon. He was not a warlike prince: he never did any feats of arms. It has been said he would have been a warrior, if he had had enemies; it might have been so: but the words more properly apply to Christ, who is King of kings, and Lord of lords; whose sword with two edges, proceeding from his mouth, cuts all his adversaries to pieces. <div eID="gen20072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20073" type="x-p"/> With thy glory and thy majesty - Be as war-like as thou art glorious and majestic. Solomon's court was splendid, and his person was majestic. These words may be well said of him. But the majesty and glory of Christ are above all: he is higher than all the kings of the earth; and has a name above every name; and at it every knee shall bend, and every tongue confess.
entries.8a0e52b122a92efbfe7fc3eebd58c51190dbe02a: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen20073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20074" type="x-p"/> In thy majesty ride prosperously - These words cannot be spoken of Solomon; they are true only of Christ. His riding is the prosperous progress of his Gospel over the earth. He uses no sword but the sword of the Spirit; and what religion, system of truth, pretended or real, ever made such progress as the religion of Christ has done, without one sword being ever drawn to propagate it from the first introduction of Christianity to the present time? His Gospel is Truth, proclaiming Humility, ענוה anvah, and Righteousness. This, indeed, is the sum of the Gospel; and an epitome of its operations in the hearts of men. <div eID="gen20074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20075" type="x-p"/> 1. The Gospel is a revelation of eternal Truth, in opposition to all false systems of religion, and to all flgurative and ceremonial representations of the true religion. It is truth concerning God, his Nature, and his Works. It is truth concerning Man, his Origin, his Intents, his Duties, and his End. It is truth in what it says concerning the natural, the moral, and the invisible world. <div eID="gen20075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20076" type="x-p"/> 2. It teaches the doctrine of meekness or Humility; opposes pride and vain glory; strips man of his assumed merits; proclaims and enforces the necessity of humiliation or repentance because of sin, humiliation under the providential hand of God, and humility in imitation of the character of the Lord Jesus Christ throughout life. <div eID="gen20076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20077" type="x-p"/> 3. The Gospel teaches Righteousness: shows the nature of sin, wrong, injustice, transgression, etc.; works righteousness in the heart; and directs and influences to the practice of it in all the actions of life. The Gospel leads him who is under its influences to give to all their due; to God, to his neighbor, to himself. And it is by the propagation of truth, humility, and righteousness, that the earth has become so far blessed, and the kingdom of Christ become extended among men. <div eID="gen20077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20078" type="x-p"/> And thy right hand shall teach thee terrible things - The Chaldee is different: "And the Lord will teach thee to perform terrible things by thy right hand." The Arabic: "And with admiration shall thy right hand direct thee." The Septuagint: "And thy right hand shall lead thee wonderfully." To the same purpose are the Vulgate, Anglo-Saxon, and the old Psalter. The meaning is, Nothing shall be able to resist thee, and the judgments which thou shalt inflict on thine enemies shall be terrible.
entries.dc773aa25c8d09c47163991efe9ca855d0ab8100: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen20078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20079" type="x-p"/> Thine arrows are sharp - The arrows here may mean the convictions produced in the hearts of men by the preaching of the Gospel. The King is God himself; his enemies are sinners of all sorts. The people, the Jews, thousands of whom were pricked in their hearts under the preaching of Peter and others. All fall before Christ; those who received the word rose again by repentance and faith; those who did not, fell down-all down!
entries.38dbce61ea083b42375696df27c9c3cfc46bd915: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen20079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20080" type="x-p"/> Thy throne, O God, is for ever - כסאך אלהים עולם ועד kisacha Elohim olam vaed. "O God, thy throne is for ever, and eternal!" The word Elohim here is the very first term or name by which the Supreme God has made himself known to the children of men. See <reference osisRef="Gen.1.1">Gen 1:1</reference>; and this very verse the apostle, <reference osisRef="Heb.1.8">Heb 1:8</reference>, has applied to Jesus Christ. On this I shall make a very short remark, but it shall be conclusive: If the apostle did not believe Jesus Christ to be the true and eternal God, he has utterly misapplied this Scripture. <div eID="gen20080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20081" type="x-p"/> The translation in the old Psalter, and the paraphrase will, on this controverted text, be considered of some importance: Thi settil God in werld of werlde: wande of ryghtyng wande of thi kyngedome. Here he loues [celebrates] God Crist - of dome. Thi settil of demyng and of kynges pouste. God es werld of werld for al that he demes es noght chaunged and that byfalles the, for the wande that es ceptre and the governyng of thi kyngdom es wande of ryghtyng, that ryghtes croked men this es the wand of goddes evenes that ay es ryght and never croked that reules ryghtwis men ard smytes wiked men. The reader will observe a blank space between the word Crist and of dome: it is the same in the original. A word has been so carefully erased with the scalpel in the above place, that not a vestige of a letter is left. From the following words I should suspect it to have been kynge or lard. Here he praises God, Christ, king of judgment. However this may be, it is evident that this ancient commentator understood the word God to be applied to Christ. I have given the sentence as it is pointed in the original.
entries.55b445c6ea6aa50dd97f50f1816bb951425d6c0e: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen20081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20082" type="x-p"/> Oil of gladness - As an evidence that all causes of mourning, sorrow, and death, were at an end; as in the state of mourning the ancients did not anoint themselves. <div eID="gen20082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20083" type="x-p"/> I have mentioned above that the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, <reference osisRef="Heb.1.8">Heb 1:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.1.9">Heb 1:9</reference>, quotes <reference osisRef="Psa.45.6">Psa 45:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.45.7">Psa 45:7</reference>, of this Psalm. I shall subjoin the substance of what I have written on these verses in that place: - <reference osisRef="Heb.1.8">Heb 1:8</reference> <div eID="gen20083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20084" type="x-p"/> Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever - If this be said of the Son of God, i.e., Jesus Christ, then Jesus Christ must be God; and indeed the design of the apostle is to prove this. The words here quoted are taken from <reference osisRef="Psa.45.6">Psa 45:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.45.7">Psa 45:7</reference>, which the ancient Chaldee paraphrast, and the most intelligent rabbins, refer to the Messiah. On the third verse of this Psalm, 'Thou art fairer than the children of men,' the Targum says: 'Thy beauty, מלכא משיחא malca Meshicha, O King Messiah, is greater than the children of men.' Aben Ezra says: 'This Psalm speaks of David, or rather of his Son the Messiah, for this is his name, <reference osisRef="Eze.34.24">Eze 34:24</reference> : And David my servant shall be a prince over them for ever.' Other rabbins confirm this opinion. "This verse is very properly considered a proof, and indeed a strong one, of the divinity of Christ; but some late versions of the New Testament have endeavored to avoid the evidence of this proof by translating the word thus: 'God is thy throne for ever and ever;' and if this version be correct, it is certain that the text can be no proof of the doctrine. Mr. Wakefield vindicates this translation at large in his History of Opinions; and ὁ Θεος being the nominative case is supposed to be sufficient justification of this version. In answer to this it may be stated that the nominative case is often used for the vocative, particularly by the Attics, and the whole scope of the place requires it should be so used here; and with due deference to all of a contrary opinion, the original Hebrew cannot be consistently translated any other way; כסאך אלהים עולם ועד kisacha Elohim olam vaed, 'Thy throne, O God, is for ever and to eternity.' It is in both worlds, and extends over all time, and will exist through all endless duration. To this our Lord seems to refer, <reference osisRef="Mat.28.18">Mat 28:18</reference> : 'All power is given unto me, both in Heaven and Earth.' My throne, i.e., my dominion, extends from the creation to the consummation of all things. These I have made, and these I uphold; and from the end of the world, throughout eternity, I shall have the same glory - sovereign unlimited power and authority, which I had with the Father before the world began; <reference osisRef="Joh.17.5">Joh 17:5</reference>. I may add that none of the ancient Versions has understood it in the way contended for by those who deny the Godhead of Christ, either in the Psalm from which it is taken, or in this place where it is quoted. Aquila translates אלהים Elohim, by Θεε, O God, in the vocative case; and the Arabic adds the sign of the vocative ya, reading the place thus: korsee yallaho ila abadilabada, the same as in our Version. And even allowing that ὁ Θεος here is to be used as the nominative case, it will not make the sense contended for without adding εστι to it, a reading which is not countenanced by any Version, nor by any MS. yet discovered. Wiclif, Coverdale, and others, understood it as the nominative, and translated it so; and yet it is evident that this nominative has the power of the vocative: Forsothe to the sone God thi troone into the world of worlde: a gerde of equite the gerde of thi reume. I give this, pointing and all, as it stands in my old MS. Bible. Wiclif is nearly the same, but is evidently of a more modern cast: But to the sone he seith, God thy trone is unto the world of world, a gherd of equyte is the gherd of thi rewme. Coverdale translates it thus: 'But unto the sonne he sayeth: God, thi seate endureth for ever and ever: the cepter of thy kyngdome is a right cepter.' Tindal and others follow in the same way, all reading it in the nominative case, with the force of the vocative; for none of them has inserted the word εστι is, because not authorized by the original; a word which the opposers of the Divinity of our Lord are obliged to beg, in order to support their interpretation. <div eID="gen20084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20085" type="x-p"/> A scepter of righteousness - The scepter, which was a sort of staff or instrument of various forms, was the ensign of government, and is here used for government itself. This the ancient Jewish writers understand also of the Messiah. <reference osisRef="Heb.1.9">Heb 1:9</reference> <div eID="gen20085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20086" type="x-p"/> Thou hast loved righteousness - This is the characteristic of a just governor; he abhors and suppresses iniquity; he countenances and supports righteousness and truth. <div eID="gen20086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20087" type="x-p"/> Therefore God, even thy God - The original, δια τουτου εχρισε δε, ὁ Θεος, ὁ Θεος σου, may be thus translated: 'Therefore, O God, thy God hath anointed thee.' The form of speech is nearly the same with that in the preceding verse; but the sense is sufficiently clear if we read: 'Therefore God, thy God, hath anointed thee,' etc. <div eID="gen20087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20088" type="x-p"/> With the oil of gladness - We have often had occasion to remark that anciently kings, priests, and prophets, were consecrated to their several offices by anointing, and that this signified the gifts and influences of the Divine Spirit. Christ, ὁ χριστος, signifies The anointed One, the same as the Hebrew Messiah; and he is here said to be 'anointed with the oil of gladness above his fellows.' None was ever constituted prophet, priest, and king, but himself: some were kings only, prophets only, and priests only; others were kings and priests, or priests and prophets, or kings and prophets; but none had ever the three offices in his own person but Jesus Christ; and none but himself can be a King over the universe, a Prophet to all intelligent beings, and a Priest to the whole human race. Thus he is infinitely exalted beyond his fellows - all that had ever borne the regal, prophetic, or sacerdotal offices. "Some think that the word μετοχους, fellows, refers to believers who are made partakers of the same Spirit, but cannot have its infinite plenitude. The first sense seems the best. Gladness is used to express the festivities which took place on the inauguration of kings," etc.
entries.b516b98e3d5247dd3ee6ce15aab2728c42144384: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen20088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20089" type="x-p"/> All thy garments smell of myrrh - The Asiatics are very partial to perfumes; every thing with them is perfumed, and especially their garments. And the ivory palaces mentioned are the wardrobes inlaid with ivory, in which their numerous changes of raiment were deposited. Myrrh and aloes are well known; cassia is probably the bark or wood of the cinnamon tree. These with frankincense, galbanum and other odoriferous drugs, were and are frequently used in the perfumes of the Asiatic nations. <div eID="gen20089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20090" type="x-p"/> Whereby they have made thee glad - Referring to the effect of strong perfumes refreshing and exhilarating the spirits.
entries.7939f3dcff2cce6078e3738979eaa3e37ace2460: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen20090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20091" type="x-p"/> Kings' daughters were among - Applied to Solomon, these words have no difficulty. We know he had seven hundred wives, princesses; and the mention of those here may be intended only to show how highly respected he was among the neighboring sovereigns, when they cheerfully gave him their daughters to constitute his harem.
